strengths: The paper provides a valuable theoretical characterization of diagonal loading for the Densest k-Subgraph (DkS) continuous relaxation, establishing that lambda = 1 is the minimal parameter value ensuring tightness.

The optimization landscape analysis is insightful: Lemma 1 and Theorem 5 formally show that for lambda > 1 all local maxima are integral and that increasing lambda only creates additional local maxima without removing existing ones, explaining why an over-regularized formulation performs worse.
The proposed Frank-Wolfe algorithm is simple, projection-free, and computationally efficient, solving the linear subproblem over the capped simplex in O(m + k log n) time per iteration.

Extensive empirical evaluations across several large-scale real-world graphs (up to millions of vertices and over 100M edges) show that the Frank-Wolfe approach achieves competitive or superior subgraph density while running significantly faster than baseline methods like EXPP and L-ADMM.
weaknesses: Technical error in the proof of Theorem 4 (Appendix B): In equation (33), the proof applies Lagrange multipliers to f(x) = x^T A x rather than the actual objective g(x) = x^T (A + lambda I) x, incorrectly claiming that partial f / partial x_1 = partial f / partial x_2. The first-order optimality condition for g(x) includes the gradient of the diagonal loading term (2 lambda x_i), which invalidates the subsequent step in equation (34) unless properly corrected.

Incorrect complexity analysis in Section 3.3: The authors claim that computing the gradient of the parameterized objective requires forming the explicit n x n Jacobian matrix J, resulting in an O(n^2) computational cost. This is incorrect: because of the rank-one plus diagonal structure of the softmax/scaling map, the vector-Jacobian product can be computed in O(n) time, yielding an O(m + n) total complexity per iteration. This theoretical misconception directly contradicts the fact that their PyTorch implementation scales to graphs with over 3 million vertices.

Incomplete referencing and relation to prior work: Reference [48] (Q. Lu, N. D. Sidiropoulos, and A. Konar, 'Densest k-subgraph mining via a provably tight relaxation', AAAI 2025) is listed in the bibliography but is never cited or discussed in the text. The relationship, overlap, and distinct contributions relative to this closely related publication must be explicitly clarified.
The manuscript does not adhere to standard conference formatting guidelines (it is set in IEEE two-column journal format).

strengths: Strong and rigorous theoretical foundation: The paper cleanly determines the exact threshold for the diagonal loading parameter (lambda = 1) that guarantees tightness of the continuous relaxation over the sum-to-k polytope. Theorem 2 sharpens prior work (Barman, 2018) from lambda = 2 to lambda >= 1, and Theorem 4 generalizes the foundational Motzkin-Straus theorem to diagonally loaded quadratic forms to establish the lower bound.

Insightful optimization landscape analysis: Lemma 1 and Theorem 5 provide formal justification for using the minimal tight parameter lambda = 1 by proving that larger values of lambda introduce additional, spurious local maxima, explaining why 'light' diagonal loading produces superior empirical results compared to heavy regularization.

Highly scalable and projection-free algorithmic design: The proposed Frank-Wolfe framework avoids the expensive Euclidean projection onto the sum-to-k constraint polytope C_k^n, achieving a per-iteration computational complexity of O(m + k log n).

Thorough and convincing empirical evaluation: The method is validated on standard large-scale benchmarks ranging up to millions of nodes and over 100 million edges (e.g., com-Orkut), consistently finding denser subgraphs with significantly lower runtimes compared to advanced baselines such as L-ADMM, EXPP, and LRBO.
weaknesses: Flawed complexity claim for the parameterization method: Section 3.3 claims that computing the gradient of the parameterized unconstrained objective requires O(n^2) time due to constructing the full n x n Jacobian matrix J. However, evaluating the gradient in reverse-mode automatic differentiation (or manually via vector-Jacobian products) requires only O(m + n) time and O(n) memory without ever explicitly forming J.

Lack of global optimality guarantees for non-convex solvers: While the relaxation itself is proven to be tight at lambda = 1, the continuous problem remains non-convex. The Frank-Wolfe algorithm and AdamW only guarantee convergence to stationary points, meaning empirical performance relies on local convergence heuristics.

Under-specified rounding post-processing: Because non-integral stationary points can arise when lambda = 1, the authors apply post-processing to obtain a binary solution. It is not entirely clear from Section 4.3 whether the post-processing uses the constructive deterministic rounding procedure outlined in Appendix A or a simple top-k projection.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis of the diagonal loading relaxation: The paper establishes that $\lambda = 1$ is the exact minimal diagonal loading parameter ensuring tightness of the continuous relaxation for DkS, improving upon the existing bound of $\lambda = 2$ by Barman (2018).

Novel extension of the Motzkin-Straus theorem: The derivation of the lower bound via an extension of the classic Motzkin-Straus theorem to $\lambda \in [0, 1]$ on the probability simplex provides an elegant theoretical justification for the sharpness of $\lambda = 1$.

Optimization landscape characterization: Theorem 5 and Lemma 1 theoretically show that increasing $\lambda > 1$ only creates additional spurious local maxima, providing a clear mathematical rationale for choosing the minimal valid parameter $\lambda = 1$.

Scalability and computational efficiency: The Frank-Wolfe algorithm avoids expensive projections onto the sum-to-$k$ polytope, requiring only a top-$k$ gradient selection ($O(m + k \log n)$ per iteration), enabling execution on graphs with millions of vertices and over 100 million edges.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty of the Frank-Wolfe method: Applying Frank-Wolfe to quadratic objectives over the capped simplex/cardinality polytope is standard, and convergence of FW to stationary points in non-convex settings is known (e.g., Lacoste-Julien, 2016).

Underwhelming contribution of the parameterization approach: The explicit constraint parameterization with AdamW incurs an $O(n^2)$ per-iteration Jacobian computation when the constraint is active, scaling poorly and underperforming Frank-Wolfe across almost all benchmarks, which weakens its utility as a core contribution.

Lack of global approximation guarantees: While the relaxation is tight at the global optimum, the problem remains non-convex and NP-hard, meaning first-order stationary points found by Frank-Wolfe lack theoretical approximation guarantees relative to the optimal density.
Formatting discrepancy: The submission is prepared in an IEEE journal/transactions two-column format spanning 12 pages rather than the standard ICML conference format.

strengths: The theoretical characterization of the diagonal loading parameter is clean and insightful: the authors prove that $\lambda = 1$ is the exact threshold for relaxation tightness by improving Barman's upper bound (from $\lambda = 2$ to $\lambda = 1$) and establishing a matching lower bound via a novel extension of the classic Motzkin-Straus theorem.

The landscape analysis (Lemma 1 and Theorem 5) provides a compelling justification for keeping $\lambda$ as small as possible (i.e., $\lambda = 1$) rather than standard convexification ($\lambda \ge -\lambda_n(A)$), proving that increasing $\lambda$ monotonically introduces spurious local maxima.

The Frank-Wolfe adaptation for this non-convex relaxation is simple, projection-free, and computationally lightweight, requiring only a top-$k$ selection per iteration ($O(m + n)$ average per-iteration complexity).

Empirical evaluations across diverse real-world benchmarks (up to millions of nodes and over 100M edges) show that the Frank-Wolfe approach consistently outperforms or matches state-of-the-art baselines in density while offering superior computational scalability.
weaknesses: The parameterization approach via AdamW feels poorly motivated and underperforming compared to Frank-Wolfe; as noted in the complexity analysis, computing the Jacobian introduces $O(n^2)$ overhead when the constraint binds, which heavily impairs scalability and solution quality.
In Section 4.3, the sentence 'Code is available at' abruptly ends without providing a repository or anonymized link.

The tightness lower bound in Corollary 2 is established specifically in the regime $k < \omega$; the necessity of $\lambda = 1$ for tightness when $k \ge \omega$ remains an open question and warrants deeper discussion.
The empirical results are reported for a single deterministic initialization without testing sensitivity to different initialization schemes or reporting variance over multiple initializations.

strengths: Clear and theoretically sound contribution on the tightness of diagonal loading: The paper establishes that $\lambda = 1$ is the exact minimal diagonal loading parameter ensuring the continuous relaxation of the Densest $k$-Subgraph (DkS) problem is tight for general $k$, nicely closing the gap left by prior work (which established tightness only for $\lambda = 2$).

Insightful optimization landscape analysis: Theorem 5 rigorously demonstrates that increasing $\lambda$ beyond 1 only adds (and never removes) local maxima, providing a clear theoretical justification for avoiding overly aggressive diagonal loading (such as enforcing positive semidefiniteness of $A + \lambda I$).

Highly scalable and practical Frank–Wolfe formulation: Exploiting the fact that the linear maximization subproblem over the capped simplex admits an exact $O(n)$ top-$k$ solution allows the Frank–Wolfe method to scale seamlessly to networks with millions of vertices and over a hundred million edges.

Thorough experimental validation: The proposed Frank–Wolfe approach consistently matches or exceeds the solution density of competitive baselines (such as L-ADMM and EXPP) while requiring significantly lower runtime on large real-world benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited practical impact of the parameterization method: The explicit parameterization via AdamW incurs an $O(n^2)$ per-iteration cost when the constraint is active and underperforms Frank–Wolfe across the board, making its inclusion somewhat secondary to the main narrative.

Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: Applying Frank–Wolfe to quadratic programming over the convex hull of cardinality constraints is a standard technique in constrained optimization; the main novelty lies in the theoretical characterization of $\lambda$ rather than the algorithm itself.
Incomplete reproducibility details: On page 14, Section 4.3 states 'Code is available at' but leaves the sentence unfinished without providing a link or repository.

strengths: Sound and elegant theoretical analysis: The paper establishes that the continuous relaxation of the Densest k-Subgraph (DkS) problem with diagonal loading is tight for $\lambda \ge 1$ (extending Barman's result where $\lambda = 2$) and proves that $\lambda = 1$ is the minimal threshold for general graphs when $k < \omega$ via a non-trivial generalization of the classic Motzkin–Straus theorem.

Insightful optimization landscape characterization: The authors show that for $\lambda > 1$ there are no non-integral local maxima, and that increasing $\lambda$ can only introduce additional spurious local maxima (Theorem 5). This provides a solid mathematical justification for choosing the minimal loading parameter $\lambda = 1$ instead of large values that convexify the objective.

Efficient, scalable algorithm: The proposed Frank–Wolfe formulation circumvents projection onto the polytope $C_k^n$, reducing the per-iteration cost to $O(m + n)$ through simple top-$k$ selection. This allows the method to scale effortlessly to massive real-world networks with millions of vertices and over 100 million edges.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments on diverse real-world benchmarks show that Frank–Wolfe with $\lambda = 1$ consistently finds denser subgraphs than existing continuous relaxation methods (e.g., EXPP, L-ADMM) and spectral methods (LRBO) while being significantly faster and less memory-intensive.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: While the theoretical characterization of diagonal loading is original and insightful, the primary algorithmic tool—applying the Frank–Wolfe algorithm to a non-convex quadratic program over a capped simplex polytope—is a standard optimization technique where the linear subproblem corresponds to simple top-$k$ selection.

Limited effectiveness of the parameterization approach: The continuous unconstrained parameterization (Section 3.2) trained via AdamW incurs higher computational complexity ($O(n^2)$ or PyTorch tensor overhead) and generally underperforms the Frank–Wolfe baseline, leaving its practical utility somewhat marginal.

Scope of the tightness lower bound: Corollary 2 proves that $\lambda \ge 1$ is necessary for tightness specifically in the regime $k < \omega$ (where $\omega$ is the clique number). In graphs where $k > \omega$, the necessity of $\lambda = 1$ is left open theoretically.
Minor presentation flaw: At the end of Section 4.3 (page 14), the sentence 'Code is available at' is left unfinished without an anonymous link or placeholder.
